title: An Ariadne's thread for SGA 4, SGA 4½ and SGA 5

pages.title: An Ariadne's thread for SGA 4, SGA 4½ and SGA 5

blocks.html: An Ariadne's thread for SGA 4, SGA 4½ and SGA 5

Exposés I to VI of SGA 4 give the general theory of Grothendieck topologies. Very detailed, they can be invaluable in the study of exotic topologies, such as the one which gives rise to crystalline cohomology. For the étale topology, so close to classical intuition, so imposing a guard-rail is not necessary: it suffices to know (for example) the book of Godement [4], and to have a little faith. Other possible references: chapters I to III of Artin's notes [1], Giraud's Bourbaki exposé [3] or [Arcata] I. Exposés VII and VIII begin the study of the étale topology. They are more detailed than Artin's chapter III and than [Arcata] II.

The study of curves is the key to étale cohomology. It is begun by Artin in exposé IX of SGA 4; some consequences, concerning cohomological dimension, are given in X. The essential points are taken up again in [Arcata] III. Exposé XI is not necessary for the sequel; it contains an elegant proof of the comparison theorem between étale and classical cohomology in the particular case of smooth complex algebraic varieties.

Exposés XII and XIII prove the fundamental base change theorem for a proper morphism. As Artin remarked in (algebraic approximation of structures over complete local rings, Publ. Math. IHES 36 (1969) p. 23-58-§3), his approximation theorem makes it possible to simplify the proof. This route is followed in [Arcata] IV, where the many dévissages of the proof are only sketched, and where the applications of exposé XIV are only very briefly indicated. The theorem makes it possible to define “cohomology with compact supports”, and the functors “higher direct images with proper supports” \(R^if_!\) (whose properties reduce to those of the higher direct image functors for a proper morphism). This is the subject of the prolix exposé XVII; the essentials are said in [Arcata] IV, but pieces of XVII may have an independent usefulness.

Exposés XV and XVI are centered on the fundamental theorem of local acyclicity for smooth morphisms. The influence of SGA 7 shows through in the less detailed parallel exposé [Arcata] V, which also contains the proof of the results required from SGA 2.

Exposé [Arcata] VI is devoted to Poincaré duality; it is clearer than SGA 4 XVIII but does not claim to give a complete proof. For those who insist on a purely algebraic proof, it is simplified by a reference to [Dualité] §3; it does not contain the proof of the formalism obeyed by the trace morphism (XVIII §2).

There exists in étale cohomology a duality formalism analogous to that of coherent cohomology. To establish it, Grothendieck used resolution of singularities and the purity conjecture (for the statement, see [Cycle] 2.1.4), established in a relative setting in SGA 4 XVI, and – modulo resolution – in equal characteristic in SGA 4 XIX. The key points are established by another method, in [Th. finitude], for schemes of finite type over a regular scheme of dimension 0 or 1. Various developments are given in SGA 5 I. In SGA 5 III, it is shown how this formalism implies the very general Lefschetz-Verdier trace formula.

One sees that in the original version of SGA 5, the Lefschetz-Verdier formula was established only conjecturally. Moreover, the local terms were not computed there. For the application to \(L\)-functions, this seminar contains another proof, this one complete, in the particular case of the Frobenius morphism. It is the one which appears in [Rapport]. Other references: for the statement and the scheme of the dévissages: Grothendieck's Bourbaki exposé [5]; for a brief description of the reduction (due to Grothendieck) of the crucial case to a case already treated by Weil, [2] §10; for an \(\ell\)-adic treatment of this last case, [Cycle] §3.

In SGA 5, one will also find a detailed treatment of the passage from \(\mathbf{Z}/\ell^n\)-cohomology to \(\mathbf{Z}_\ell\)-cohomology (exposés V and VI, by J.P. Jouanolou), and of the formalism of the Frobenius morphism (exposé XV, by C. Houzel). Exposés X and XII, written by I. Bucur, give the computation of the Euler-Poincaré characteristic of a sheaf on a curve, and that of the trace of the endomorphism of its cohomology defined by certain correspondences. In VII, Jouanolou gives the computation of the cohomology of classical schemes, and applications. Moreover, Serre's exposé “Introduction à la théorie de Brauer” has been taken up in his book [6] (part 3).
